content: The initial scope of the guideline was drafted, and priority questions were identified using the PICO format, which includes population, intervention, comparators, and outcomes. A guideline planning proposal was prepared, and systematic review teams, a guideline methodologist, and members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) were identified and invited. The evidence retrieval, assessment, and synthesis processes were supervised, GDG meetings were organized, draft recommendations were prepared for GDG consideration, the final guideline document was compiled, and the publication and dissemination of the guideline were managed. The WHO Steering Group selected 25 external experts and stakeholders from six WHO regions to form the GDG. Selection criteria included geographic representation, gender balance, and the absence of conflicts of interest. The GDG was a diverse group with expertise in research, clinical practice, policy, program development, guideline methodology, and service delivery approaches, including patient and consumer representatives. The GDG participated in a virtual scoping meeting with the Steering Group in December 2020, providing input on the PICO questions and related details to guide evidence reviews. Between November 2021 and January 2022, GDG members reviewed and interpreted evidence, formulated the wording of final recommendations, and provided remarks and considerations during virtual meetings. They also reviewed and approved the final guideline document. The External Review Group (ERG) consisted of four technical experts and stakeholders with experience in the care of preterm or low-birth-weight (LBW) infants. This group was geographically representative and gender-balanced. The ERG peer-reviewed the draft guideline document after GDG approval, assessing it for factual errors, clarity of language, decision-making processes, values and preferences of affected individuals (families, health workers, managers, and policymakers), and implementation implications. However, the ERG was not authorized to alter recommendations formulated by the GDG. The Evidence Synthesis Team (EST) included the guideline methodologist, systematic review teams, and members of the WHO Steering Group. They appraised the quality of existing systematic reviews, commissioned new reviews and structured searches, and prepared GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) frameworks for each priority question. EST members also attended GDG meetings to present evidence and support discussions. Representatives from UNICEF, Save the Children, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the International Pediatric Association (IPA), and USAID were invited to GDG meetings as observers. These organizations, with a history of collaboration with WHO, are potential partners in guideline implementation. Observers could provide comments during technical discussions but did not participate in final recommendation discussions. In line with WHO procedures, all GDG, EST, and ERG members, as well as other external contributors, were required to declare any competing interests (academic, financial, or other) in writing before engaging in the guideline development process. Declarations of interest (DOIs) were reviewed by the WHO Steering Group to identify and manage potential conflicts of interest. No declared interests were deemed serious enough to compromise the guideline development process or its credibility. Experts with primary research related to specific recommendations were restricted from participating in discussions or formulating recommendations in those areas. A summary of the DOIs and their management is provided in Annex 3. The DECIDE (Developing and Evaluating Communication strategies to support Informed Decisions and practice based on Evidence) approach was used to guide evidence search, synthesis, and judgments by the EST, as well as the formulation of recommendations by the GDG. Evidence on the effectiveness of interventions was primarily derived from systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). If RCT reviews were unavailable, systematic reviews of non-randomized studies were used. All commissioned systematic reviews followed standard methods, including pre-published protocols, clear PICO questions, and rigorous data analysis plans. The GRADE approach was employed to assess the quality and certainty of quantitative evidence for each priority question. Evidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty. RCTs were considered high-certainty evidence, while non-randomized trials and observational studies were rated as low-certainty evidence. The GRADE-CERQual tool was used to appraise qualitative evidence, focusing on values, acceptability, and feasibility. The GDG reviewed EtD frameworks, draft recommendations, and feedback during virtual meetings. Discussions included evidence presentation, consideration of EtD domains, and deliberations on the direction, strength, and conditions of each recommendation. Consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the GDG, was reached for all recommendations, with no strong disagreements. Research gaps and implications were also identified. Following the final GDG meeting, the WHO technical officer prepared a draft of the full guideline document, reflecting GDG deliberations and decisions. The draft was reviewed by the WHO Steering Group, GDG members, and ERG peer reviewers. Revisions were made to address factual errors, improve clarity, and align with WHO style. The final recommendations are presented in the guideline's executive summary and detailed in Chapter 3, along with background information, evidence summaries, and GDG remarks. Recommendations were categorized into preventive and promotive care, care for complications, and family involvement and support. Strong recommendations were phrased as is recommended or should receive, while conditional recommendations were phrased as may be considered. Good practice statements were included for interventions deemed obviously beneficial despite limited evidence. The guideline includes 11 new recommendations, 14 updated recommendations, and one new good practice statement.
